title: Albariño
description: Also called Alvarinho in Portugal. A crisp, saline, peach-scented white of the Atlantic north-west of Iberia.
L: Albariño gives crisp whites with lemon, grapefruit, white peach, apricot, white flowers and a saline, mineral edge. Acidity is high, body light to medium. It's aromatic yet dry. Its home is the Atlantic coast of north-west Spain and northern Portugal.

Albariño has small berries with thick skins, which resist mildew and rot in its wet, humid homeland. Thick skins also hold aromatic compounds, giving its perfume, and can add a slightly bitter, phenolic finish. Some producers use skin contact or lees ageing for extra texture.
Thick skins for a wet climate
Why does Albariño suit its wet, Atlantic home?
Its thick skins resist mildew and rot

Look for pale lemon colour, peach and citrus aromas, and a crisp, saline, mineral palate. Compared with Sauvignon Blanc, it's more stone fruit and less green; compared with Viognier, lighter and much fresher.
Albariño has thin skins that make it prone to rot.
Not true. Its thick skins help it resist rot.
Albariño gives peach, citrus and a saline edge
Thick skins resist rot in a wet climate

Rías Baixas, in Galicia, Spain's Atlantic north-west, is about 96% Albariño. It's named after the rías, flooded river valleys. Rainfall is high, 1,600 mm or more a year. Five sub-zones include Val do Salnés, coolest and most Atlantic, and O Rosal and Condado do Tea, warmer, along the Miño river. Granite soils dominate.

To fight humidity, vines are traditionally trained on high pergolas, called parras, on granite posts, two metres or more above the ground. Air circulates under the canopy, reducing rot; grapes stay away from damp soil. Some growers now use wire trellises, which allow more sun on the fruit.
Match each Rías Baixas term to its meaning.
Rías Baixas' landscape shapes its wine.
Across the Miño, called Minho in Portugal, Albariño is called Alvarinho. It grows in Vinho Verde, especially in Monção e Melgaço. Spain and Portugal share the grape, divided by a river.
Why are Albariño vines trained on high pergolas?
To let air circulate and reduce rot
Rías Baixas is about 96% Albariño on granite
Across the river, Portugal calls it Alvarinho
Explain the role of lees ageing

Spanish Albariño from Rías Baixas is crisp, peachy and saline, usually unoaked, around 12.5 to 13%. Portuguese Alvarinho from Monção e Melgaço, a warmer, sheltered sub-region of Vinho Verde, is often fuller and riper, with tropical notes. Both share the grape's acidity and perfume.

Monção e Melgaço, on the south bank of the Minho, is protected from the Atlantic by hills, so it's warmer and drier than the rest of Vinho Verde. Alvarinho there reaches higher ripeness and gives Vinho Verde's most serious whites. Unlike most Vinho Verde, they're rarely spritzy.
Why is Monção e Melgaço warmer than the rest of Vinho Verde?
Hills shelter it from the Atlantic
Shelter from Atlantic winds and rain gives more warmth.

Many producers age Albariño on its lees for months, adding texture and creaminess. Some use oak or concrete. Though usually drunk young, good Albariño and Alvarinho can age five to ten years, gaining honey and toasted notes while keeping their acidity.
Which describe Monção e Melgaço Alvarinho?
Monção e Melgaço Alvarinho is rarely spritzy.
Rías Baixas Albariño is crisp and saline
Monção e Melgaço Alvarinho is riper and fuller
Lees ageing adds texture; good examples age
Know how long to keep it

Albariño is Galicia's seafood wine: pulpo a la gallega, octopus with paprika, mussels, scallops, clams, oysters and grilled fish. Its acidity and saline edge match the sea. It also suits ceviche, sushi and light Asian dishes.
Serve at 8 to 10 degrees. Most is best within two to three years. Lees-aged and top examples can age five to ten years. In Galicia, it's often served in a white ceramic cup, a cunca, for local wines.
Which Galician dish is a classic match for Albariño?
Octopus with paprika and olive oil suits Albariño's acidity and salinity.
Albariño with a plate of mussels or oysters is about as close to a perfect pairing as it gets.
Most Albariño is best drunk within two to three years.
Yes, though top examples can age longer.
Albariño suits octopus, shellfish and ceviche
